name: THE WHAT WE DILL IN THE SHADOWS BURGER

recipe.history:
Dill — Anethum graveolens — is one of the oldest cultivated herbs in human history, with records of its use dating back more than five thousand years to ancient Egypt, where it was found in the tomb of Amenhotep II and prescribed in medical papyri as a digestive aid. The herb takes its name from the Old Norse word 'dilla,' meaning to soothe or lull, a reference to its traditional use as a calming remedy for infant colic. Dill thrives in the temperate climates of Scandinavia, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, and it became a cornerstone of the culinary traditions of those regions in very different ways. In Scandinavia, dill is virtually inseparable from salmon — gravlax cured with dill, dill-butter sauces for poached fish, dill stirred into potato salads and cream sauces. In Eastern Europe, particularly in Poland, Russia, and the Baltic states, dill is added to everything: borscht, sour cream, cucumber salads, kefir-based sauces, pickles, and braised meats. The Ashkenazi Jewish tradition of pickling cucumbers in brine with copious quantities of fresh dill produced the classic New York deli pickle — the half-sour and the full-sour — that became one of the defining flavors of American Jewish cuisine and, by extension, the American deli.

Dill's path into American burger culture is inextricably linked to the pickle. The dill pickle arrived in America with Eastern European Jewish immigrants in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and the pickles sold from barrels by pushcart vendors on New York's Lower East Side became an immediate and enduring sensation. By the mid-20th century, dill pickles were the standard burger condiment at virtually every diner, drive-in, and fast food restaurant in the country — McDonald's built a national identity partly on the thin, briny dill pickle slices that topped their burgers. But dill's influence extends beyond the pickle; in recent years, the craft burger movement has embraced dill in more sophisticated applications: dill-infused aioli, dill cream sauces, dill pickle chips fried in batter, whole dill fronds as a fresh garnish. The herb's distinctive combination of grassy, slightly anise-like freshness and bright acidity makes it a natural partner for rich, fatty beef, cutting through the heaviness and refreshing the palate between bites. This burger celebrates dill in two forms — crunchy fried dill pickle chips and a luxurious dill cream sauce — honoring both its humble pickle heritage and its potential for elevation.

My relationship with dill pickles is essentially a love story that began in childhood and has never wavered. I grew up in a household where the pickle jar was a permanent fixture on the refrigerator door, always the big glass jar of whole dill pickles floating in cloudy brine, the kind you had to reach in and pull out by hand. My mother would slice them lengthwise for sandwiches and chop them for potato salad, but my favorite was to eat them whole, standing at the open refrigerator, the brine dripping on the kitchen floor. Later, as a teenager, I discovered dill in its fresh form — a sprig floating on a bowl of borscht at a friend's grandmother's house — and understood for the first time that the herb and the pickle were related but not identical. The fresh dill had a brightness and a green, almost grassy quality that the pickled version only suggested. Years later, working in a kitchen, I learned to make dill cream sauce and realized it was essentially the distillation of everything I had ever loved about the herb: tangy, fresh, rich, and deeply savory all at once.

A burger cooked to medium rare is the natural partner for bright, acidic condiments like dill cream sauce and fried pickle chips, because at that temperature — 130–135°F — the meat still has the moisture and fat to stand up to and be complemented by acidity rather than overwhelmed by it. A patty cooked beyond medium begins to tighten and dry out, losing the juiciness that makes it a worthy foil for bold toppings. When you bite into a medium rare patty topped with crunchy, vinegary pickle chips and a cool, herbaceous cream sauce, every element is in balance: the heat of the beef, the cool of the sauce, the crunch of the chip, the brine of the dill. Cook that patty to well-done and you eliminate the contrast entirely — the dried-out beef simply absorbs the sauce without giving anything back. Medium rare is not just a preference; for a burger like this, it is a structural necessity. It is the thing that makes all the other elements cohere.
ingredients: 1 tbsp dill pickle brine (from the jar)
For the fried dill pickle chips:
20–24 dill pickle rounds (store-bought or homemade, about ¼-inch thick)
For the quick dill pickles (if making from scratch):
4 Kirby cucumbers, sliced into ¼-inch rounds
4 slices white American cheese or Havarti
instructions: 1. Make quick dill pickles (if making from scratch, at least 24 hours ahead): Combine vinegar, water, salt, and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir until dissolved and remove from heat. Pack cucumber slices into a clean jar with dill sprigs, garlic, peppercorns, and dill seeds. Pour hot brine over cucumbers. Cool to room temperature, seal, and refrigerate at least 24 hours.

2. Make the sesame buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture, softened butter, and egg. Knead on medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

3. Divide dough into 6 portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and let rise 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle generously with sesame seeds. Bake 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

4. Make the dill cream sauce: Combine sour cream, mayonnaise, fresh dill, pickle brine, lemon juice, grated garlic, salt, white pepper, and whole grain mustard in a bowl. Whisk until fully combined. Taste and adjust seasoning — add more dill for herbaceous punch, more pickle brine for acidity. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

5. Prepare the fried pickle chips: Pat pickle rounds completely dry with paper towels — this is critical for crispy results. Set up a three-station breading line: (1) seasoned flour (flour, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, cayenne, salt, pepper); (2) beaten eggs; (3) panko breadcrumbs. Coat each pickle slice in flour, shake off excess, dip in egg, then press firmly into panko, ensuring full coverage.

6. Heat about 1 inch of neutral oil in a heavy skillet or saucepan to 375°F. Fry pickle chips in batches of 6–8, 1–2 minutes per side, until golden brown and crisp. Transfer to a wire rack lined with paper towels. Season immediately with salt. Work quickly — fried pickles are best eaten fresh.

7. Form burger patties: Gently mix ground beef with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties and press a shallow dimple in the center of each.

8. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Add patties and cook 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once. Add a slice of cheese to each patty immediately after flipping. Cook 1–2 more minutes until cheese is melted and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat. Toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of dill cream sauce on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Add a small handful of shredded iceberg lettuce and a few thin slices of red onion. Stack 5–6 fried dill pickle chips on top. Spoon a little extra dill cream sauce over the pickles. Add a few fresh dill fronds. Cap with the top bun, press lightly, and serve immediately while the pickle chips are still hot and crisp.
